.
Include in the subject line “NEFSC On-demand EFP.” All comments received are a part of the public record and may be posted for public viewing without change. All personal identifying information (
e.g.,
name, address), confidential business information, or otherwise sensitive information submitted voluntarily by the sender will be publicly accessible. NMFS will accept anonymous comments (enter “anonymous” as the signature if you wish to remain anonymous).
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Christine Ford, Fishery Management Specialist,
Christine.Ford@noaa.gov
,
(978) 281-9185.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
The NOAA NEFSC submitted a complete application for an EFP to conduct commercial fishing activities that the regulations would otherwise restrict, to continue trials of on-demand fishing gear that use one or no surface buoys, and to test the ability of gear marking systems to consistently locate gear. This EFP would exempt the participating vessels from the following Federal regulations:
(
printed page 64886)
Table 1—Requested Exemptions
CFR citation
Regulation
Need for exemption
50 CFR 697.21(b)
Gear marking requirements
For trial of trap/pot gear with no more than one surface marking on trawls of more than three traps, and trial of trap/pot gear with no surface marking on trawls of three or fewer traps.
50 CFR 648.84(b)
Gear marking requirements
For trial of gillnet gear with no more than one surface marking.
50 CFR 648.264(a)(5)
Gear marking requirements
For trial of red crab trap/pot gear with no more than one surface marking on trawls.
Table 2—Project Summary
Project title
Development and trials of on-demand fishing systems in fixed gear fisheries.
Project start
01/01/2027.
Project end
12/31/2027.
Project objectives
This research is designed to help fishermen test alternatives to traditional vertical buoy lines and physical gear markers in fixed gear fisheries.
Project location
Gulf of Maine, Georges Bank, Southern New England, and Mid-Atlantic including, but not limited to Statistical Areas: 511, 512, 513, 514, 515, 521, 522, 525, 526, 537, 538, 539, 561, 562, 621, and 626.
Number of vessels
Trap/pot: Up to 90, including up to 5 using grappling;
                             Gillnet: Up to 10.
Number of trips
Trap/pot: Up to 9,500 trips (90 vessels making an average of 1.5 trips/week);
                             Gillnet: Up to 1,000 trips (10 vessels making an average of 2 trips/week).
Trip duration (days)
Variable based on fishery, target species, and fishing location, but within the range of standard commercial fishing trips and consistent with FMP regulations.
Gear type(s)
Lobster traps, deep-sea red crab pots, fish pots, and anchored-fixed gillnets.
Number of tows or sets
Trap/pot: Effort capped at 900 modified trap trawls;
                             Gillnet: Effort capped at 100 modified gillnet strings. 
                             Per vessel effort will vary by season, fishing operation, and the number of active participants, but will not exceed 20 modified trawls and/or strings. 
                             In Atlantic Large Whale Take Reduction Plan (ALWTRP) Restricted Areas, effort will be limited to fully on-demand lobster trawls, fished with no persistent vertical lines. Vessels will be allowed to modify up to 20 trawls each, with a cap of 600 total trawls actively fished across the Restricted Areas.
Duration of tows or sets
Trap/pot: Variable but expected to be 14 days or less; will not exceed FMP soak limits;
                             Gillnet: typical commercial soak times.
Project Narrative
This project is a continuation of DA25-051 to trial on-demand (also known as ropeless) fishing systems aimed at reducing the entanglement risk to protected species, mainly the North Atlantic Right Whale, in trap/pot and gillnet fisheries. DA25-051 authorized on-demand gear trials on up to 180 total trap/pot vessels and up to 20 total gillnet vessels to replace up to 20 of their existing trawls/strings (up to 2,000 total trawls/strings) with modified trawls/strings, including in the ALWTRP Restricted Areas. DA25-051 expires on December 31, 2026.
This EFP would allow up to 90 total trap/pot vessels and up to 10 gillnet vessels to replace up to 20 of their existing trawls/strings (up to 1,000 total trawls/strings) with modified trawls/strings, including in the ALWTRP Restricted Areas. Modified gear would replace one or both traditional end lines with acoustic on-demand systems and other alternatives to persistent buoy lines (including, but not limited to, spooled systems, buoy and stowed-rope systems, lift-bag systems, and grappling).
The research focus for 2027 includes:
New acoustic releases, stowed rope designs, inflatable systems, and emerging technologies will be evaluated as they become available. Investigators will work with manufacturers and fishermen to test and refine gears and gather data to inform regulators. New innovative gears will be tested using hybrid, one end ropeless, configurations in areas open to commercial fishing.
New and existing on-demand gear performance will be evaluated in varied environmental conditions among varied vessel and gear configurations to inform safety decisions and refine reliability and operability. Emerging systems designed for deeper waters (>75 fathoms (137.2 meters)) will be evaluated in terms of reliability and operationally feasible.
Data analysis will focus on durability, performance, user experience, and additional criteria that could be used to later approve innovative gear technologies.
Dedicated research trips will be employed to evaluate alternative (digital) gear location marking accuracy and compare gear marking methods (manual versus automatic).
Experimental fishing in Restricted Areas will incorporate novel on-demand systems and new fishing partners to further assess the feasibility and efficiency of fishing fully on-demand trawls. Trials will be conducted with a focus on safety (protected species and fishermen) and equity (fishermen and manufacturers).
NEFSC will coordinate with Maine's Department of Marine Resources and Massachusetts' Department of Marine Fisheries on-demand research programs.
Communication efforts will continue to the broader fishing community.
To ensure that on-demand fishing and gear marking technologies are adequately tested across the breadth of regional commercial fishing conditions, NEFSC requests the flexibility to test on-demand gear across the geographic range of the Federal American lobster and Jonah crab fishery, including testing fully on-demand gear (no persistent vertical lines) in ALWTRP Restricted Areas. It also requests the opportunity to trial on-demand gillnet and other trap/pot gear across the Gulf of Maine, Georges Bank, Southern New England, and the Mid-Atlantic. To cover a greater area and target areas where data is needed, NEFSC has requested flexibility
(
printed page 64887)
to have greater than 100 participants during the permit period (with only 100 fishing at one time). It would provide requested modifications to the active participants, general locations, and technologies to be tested one month in advance. Priority would be given to participants who are seasonally excluded from fishing in certain areas and/or in offshore fisheries with limited entanglement mitigation options.
This permit would only exempt vessels from the specified Federal regulations in Federal waters. It would not exempt the vessels from any requirements imposed by any State, the Endangered Species Act, the Marine Mammal Protection Act, or any other applicable laws. The applicant would be responsible for obtaining all required State authorizations. Other than gear markings, all trap/pot trawls and gillnet strings would be consistent with the regulations of the management area where the vessel is fishing and would be fished in accordance with the participating vessels' standard operations (number and length of trips, soak times, trap limits,
etc.
).
The use of on-demand lobster trap gear in the ALWTRP Restricted Areas is limited to gear without any persistent vertical lines. The EFP would allow vessels to modify up to 20 trawls each, but would cap effort to 600 total trawls in the ALWTRP Restricted Areas. If necessary, due to a high level of interest and limited capacity, the NEFSC may require a demonstrated history of fishing within ALWTRP Restricted Areas as a condition for participation in on-demand trials in those areas.
In recognition of industry's interest in grappling as a low-cost alternative to acoustic on-demand systems, this project would allow up to 5 trap/pot vessels to retrieve up to 20 trawls via grappling; this would be a subset of the 90 total trap/pot vessels and the 900 modified trap/pot trawls effort cap. This would enable NEFSC to collect data on the viability of grappling at a commercial scale. Although no grappling trials have occurred to date, four vessels/operators have expressed interest in participating in the study. No grappling would be allowed in the ALWTRP Restricted Areas.
In phase one of participation, staff from NEFSC and the gear manufacturers would provide training to ensure that the system is working as intended and that all participants have sufficient experience with the gear before borrowing from the gear cache library. In phase two, participating vessels would rig an on-demand system to one end of a standard trawl or string and fish it as a hybrid (with one traditional surface marking) for at least 10 hauls per system. In phase three, participants would fish the gear as part of normal fishing operations, including fishing fully on-demand gear and fully on-demand trap trawls in the ALTWRP Restricted Areas. In some cases, a scientific observer may be on board, and/or GoPro Systems (or equivalent) may record gear retrievals. NEFSC would provide standardized data collection sheets to all participants, but individually identifiable data will only be made public with the express permission of the vessel owner.
NEFSC also plans to include targeted geolocation studies in areas with limited trawling and/or dredging to test new location-marking systems on the seafloor and automated location-marking when gear is set and retrieved. This EFP would support efforts to improve gear-marking and gear-conflict avoidance technologies, including testing sub-surface gear location vs. surface location where the gear is deployed, and other gear marking technologies. This EFP would also continue to test the EarthRanger and rmwHub platforms that display gear locations from various gear-marking technologies. NEFSC would demonstrate and encourage adoption of these technologies with non-participant vessels.
NEFSC proposes the following best practices and risk reduction measures for all vessels:
All vessels would report all right whale sightings to NMFS via
ne.rw.survey@noaa.gov
or (866-755-6622) or the U.S. Coast Guard (Channel 16) and record sightings on data sheets;
All vessels would retrieve on-demand vertical lines as quickly as possible to minimize time in the water column;
All vessels would provide mandatory, weekly gear loss reports;
All vessels would operate within a 10-knot (5.14 meters per second) speed limit when transiting ALWTRP Restricted Areas or when whales are observed;
For fully on-demand gear without traditional surface markings, participants would use cloud-based data aggregators to share gear locations and orientation details, which would be available to Federal, State, and corresponding enforcement personnel, as well as other fishermen in proximity to the gear;
For fully on-demand gear without traditional surface markings, on-demand vertical lines would be marked with unique orange marks above the regional markings, in addition to ALWTRP regulations (per agreement with the NMFS Atlantic Large Whale Take Reduction Team Coordinator);
When fishing in ALWTRP Restricted Areas, vessels would check real-time right whale sightings information (such as Right Whale Sightings Advisories and Whale ALERT) before setting any gear and avoid areas of high right whale abundance, and all vessels would be recommended to follow this process when setting gear outside the ALWTRP Restricted Areas;
Enforcement will be provided with and trained on digital gear marking systems prior to the start of trials, so they can locate research gear;
The NEFSC would continue to provide monthly updates on any gear conflicts to GARFO's Sustainable Fisheries Division.
Vessels fishing fully on-demand lobster trap trawls in seasonal Restricted Areas will be required to follow additional practices:
All participants will be trained by NEFSC on-demand gear experts and gear manufacturers and achieve a sufficient level of experience with the gear based on NEFSC's standard three-phase training protocol (described above) prior to Restricted Area fishing;
Participants will carry a NEFSC scientist on a subset of trips to overs trial performance and collect additional data;
An NEFSC-issued research flag will be flown by each vessel;
No floating groundline will be used on research trawls, including where otherwise legally allowed between the first trap and anchor or on-demand unit;
Project vessels will operate within a 10-knot vessel speed limit in the Restricted Areas;
If any large whale species comes within 500 yards of a participating vessel during hauling, fishing will immediately cease, by either removal or resetting, and be reinitiated only after it was reasonable to assume the whale(s) has left the area;
Participants will be provided with information on species identification as well as protocols to report live, dead, or entangled sightings of all large whale species. All whale sightings will be recorded on data sheets.
If approved, the applicant may request minor modifications and extensions to the EFP throughout the year. EFP modifications and extensions may be granted without further notice if they are deemed essential to facilitate completion of the proposed research and have minimal impacts that do not change the scope or impact of the initially approved EFP request. Any fishing activity conducted outside the
(
printed page 64888)
scope of the exempted fishing activity would be prohibited.

General Description of Collection:
Section 1828(o) of the Federal Deposit Insurance Act requires each federal banking agency to adopt uniform regulations prescribing real estate lending standards. Part 365 of the FDIC Rules and Regulations, which implements section 1828(o), requires institutions to have real estate lending policies that include (a) limits and standards consistent with safe and sound banking practices; (b) prudent underwriting standards, including loan- to-value ratio (LTV) limits that are clear and measurable; (c) loan administration policies; (d) documentation, approval and reporting requirements; and (e) a requirement for annual review and approval by the board of directors. The rule also establishes supervisory LTV limits and other underwriting considerations in the form of guidelines. There is no change in the substance or methodology of this information collection. The estimated annual burden has decreased by 8,780 hours, from 61,720 hours to 52,940 hours, due to a reduction in the number of respondents.

Project Narrative
The subject EFP application is proposed in the broader context of ongoing discussions regarding access by the surfclam fishery to historical fishing grounds in the GSC HMA, which was curtailed through the Council's Omnibus Habitat Amendment 2. The surfclam industry has since sought to re-gain access to this area, which was partially accommodated in 2020 through the Clam Dredge Framework that established three exemption areas within the GSC HMA where surfclam fishing is allowed. In addition, the Rose and Crown and Davis Bank East were informally designated as research exemption areas, and considered candidate areas where bottom tending mobile gear could be used in support of GSC HMA research priorities. The Council is currently assessing the effectiveness of the exemption area program, and may consider further changes to the GSC HMA in 2027.
The EFP applicant is proposing to assess the economic viability of the surfclam resource in the GSC HMA research exemption areas Rose and Crown and Davis Bank East, and contrast this with the surfclam resource
(
printed page 64883)
in surrounding waters outside of the HMA that are currently open to the surfclam fishery. A secondary objective is to generate a standardized spatial dataset on surfclam distribution patterns, size structure, and catch per unit effort (CPUE) within the Rose and Crown and Davis Bank East research exemption areas. The applicant states that data generated by this EFP would provide the empirical baseline needed to assess the socioeconomic impacts of the GSC HMA. Specifically, this information could contribute directly to the Council's exemption area review by filling data gaps concerning small-vessel operational viability and surfclam distribution, in support of future consideration for exemption area changes.
The applicant is requesting that 1-4 vessels be authorized to take up to 200 trips inside the Rose and Crown and Davis Bank East (test areas), to be compared with approximately 200 trips outside the HMA (control area) over the course of the 2.5-year study. If approved, the EFP would be re-issued on an annual basis, pending progress on project objectives. The same vessels, operators, and gear would fish approximately equal effort in each area. The applicant states that 400 total trips would provide a sufficient number of data points to establish commercial viability thresholds across seasonal, depth, and vessel-capacity strata. Participating vessels would land up to the equivalent of 16 cages of surfclams per trip. Control fishing would occur within Massachusetts state waters east and southeast of Cape Cod, and proximal Federal waters outside of the HMA, and test area fishing would occur within the GSC HMA Rose and Crown and Davis Bank East exemption areas. Vessels would not fish in control and test areas on the same trip.
Bushels per hour of active towing and swept area (the productivity rate metric), and pounds of shucked meat per bushel of live surfclams landed (the yield-quality metric), are the two primary metrics collected under this EFP that would be used to compare economic productivity of the control and test areas. For each tow, vessel operators and/or sea technicians would record:
Tow fishing start and end time (to the minute);
Tow speed over ground;
Start and end coordinates;
Bushels of surfclams estimated at time of sorting;
Number of cages filled and cage tag numbers (or alternate volume unit and tag numbers);
Sediment type as observed in dredge bag contents (sand, gravel, shell hash, mud, cobble);
Any notable changes in bottom composition or structure across tows; and
Species identity and estimated weight of all non-target species (bycatch).
For each trip landing under the EFP, the following will be recorded:
Total bushels of live surfclams landed;
Percentage of clams live vs. broken or damaged at time of offloading;
Ex-vessel price per bushel (market price on date of landing);
Gross ex-vessel revenue;
Pounds of shucked meat produced per bushel of live weight;
Dredge specifications (blade width, bar spacing); and
Total hours of active towing.
To assess the spatial distribution and density of surfclams in the GSC HMA Rose and Crown and Davis Bank East research exemption areas, the applicant is proposing to conduct approximately 35, 15-minute standardized tows during test area fishing trips at pre-determined station locations that follow a fixed grid design. At least one standardized tow would be occupied per exempted trip until all stations are sampled. Vessel operators would have discretion to perform the tow within 1 nautical mile of the station location to accommodate obstacles or un-towable bottom. The operator would note when the tow locations deviate from the sampling plan, and why.
Tow location, duration, total catch in bushels, and a one-bushel surfclam subsample would be recorded for each tow to characterize surfclam distribution patterns across the test areas. Vessels would use their commercial dredge to conduct standardized tows. Each surfclam in the sub-sample would be measured to the nearest 5 millimeters. The sub-sample would either be measured at sea, or separated and measured shoreside. The applicant notes that this dataset would not replace a formal fishery-independent survey, but would provide valuable information on the distribution of the surfclam resource in the test areas.
At the conclusion of each season and upon EFP expiration, the following analysis would be performed:
Productivity comparison:
Mean bushels per hour of active towing and swept area in control area trips vs. test area trips, with confidence intervals;
Meat yield comparison:
Mean pounds of shucked meat per bushel for control vs. test area landings;
Revenue-per-trip comparison:
Mean gross ex-vessel revenue per trip in control vs. test areas, controlling for trip duration and market price variation;
Summary of CPUE and catch composition from commercial tows by sub-area and depth stratum within the GSC HMA test areas;
Spatial distribution and density of surfclams by size class caught during standardized tows;
Annualized fleet-level economic impact:
Using the observed productivity differential and publicly available data on the number of small-vessel Massachusetts surfclam permit holders, estimate the aggregate annual economic loss to the fleet attributable to the GSC HMA restrictions; and
Cost-benefit framing:
Present the annualized economic cost of the closure against the available scientific literature on habitat recovery rates and the habitat protection benefit provided by excluding the small-vessel fleet.
The applicant and partner vessels would adhere to the following reporting schedule:
Trip-level data sheets and Vessel Trip Reports;
Vessel Monitoring System trip declaration using the GSC HMA EFP project code for every EFP trip;
Weekly dealer reports;
Interim progress report with preliminary economic analysis submitted to GARFO every 90 days after commencement of EFP fishing; and
Final economic impact report submitted to GARFO within 30 days of EFP expiration, summarizing productivity data, meat yield data, revenue comparisons, fleet-level economic impact estimates, spatial CPUE characterization, and recommendations regarding small-vessel access in the GSC HMA.
The final report will be made available to New England and Mid-Atlantic Fishery Management Councils, and GARFO, for review and use in future Council deliberations regarding the GSC HMA.
The applicant has also requested authorization to use alternatives to the industry-standard 32-bushel cages and cage tags. The exemption would follow the EFP issued to the Cape Cod Commercial Fisherman's Alliance (EFP #25056), which is developing alternative volume landing units more suitable to smaller surfclam vessels. Participating vessels could use two alternative landing containers: a standard-size fish vat (internal measurements: 44 inch x 39 inch x 27 inch; 1.12 meter (m) x 0.99 m x 0.69 m) capable of holding 16 bushels (0.85 m
3

3
). One alternative denomination of a 16-bushel tag would be used, either on a fish vat or on a pallet of ten 1.5-bushel totes. The applicant would work with GARFO and the National Band and Tag Company to convert standard cage tags into the alternative tag denomination.
If approved, the applicant may request minor modifications and extensions to the EFP throughout the year. EFP modifications and extensions may be granted without further notice if they are deemed essential to facilitate completion of the proposed research and have minimal impacts that do not change the scope or impact of the initially approved EFP request. Any fishing activity conducted outside the scope of the exempted fishing activity would be prohibited.

ACTION:
Final rule.
SUMMARY:
This rulemaking implements gear marking requirements and entanglement risk reduction measures for portions of the Pacific coast groundfish fishery. This rulemaking consists of mandatory requirements and voluntary measures. These new requirements and voluntary measures are established pursuant to the Magnuson-Stevens Fishery Conservation and Management Act (Magnuson-Stevens Act). The intent of the gear marking requirements is to increase the likelihood of attributing entanglements to a specific fishery and gear type. The intent of the risk reduction measures is to reduce bycatch by decreasing the likelihood of marine animal entanglements with fishing line.
DATES:

This final rule is effective January 11, 2027, with the exception of §§ 660.219(a)(1) and 660.319(a)(1), which are effective October 13, 2026.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
The Pacific Coast groundfish fishery in the U.S. exclusive economic zone (EEZ) seaward of Washington, Oregon, and California (the West Coast) is managed under the Pacific Coast Groundfish Fishery Management Plan (Groundfish FMP). This final rule implements gear marking requirements and entanglement risk reduction measures for portions of the Pacific Coast groundfish fishery. These measures are consistent with the authority provided through the Magnuson-Stevens Act section 303(a)(11) (
16 U.S.C. 1853(a)(11)
) for conservation and management measures that, to the extent practicable, minimize bycatch; and with the authority provided at Magnuson-Stevens Act section 303(b)(4) (
16 U.S.C. 1853(b)(4)
) for measures that allow for prohibiting, limiting, conditioning, or requiring use of specified types of fishing gear. The framework for gear definitions and restrictions is described in the Groundfish FMP in section 6.6, which notes that gear definitions and restrictions may be revised through a rulemaking process. Additionally, section 6.10.3 of the Groundfish FMP authorizes gear identification requirements, and provides that these requirements may be modified as necessary in Federal regulations.
This rulemaking consists of new mandatory requirements and voluntary measures and is promulgated pursuant to the Magnuson-Stevens Act section 303(c) and 304(b)(1)(A) (
16 U.S.C. 1853(c)
and
16 U.S.C. 1853(b)(1)(A)
). The intent of the gear marking requirements for buoys and portions of lines is to increase the likelihood of attributing entanglements to a specific fishery. The intent of the risk reduction measures is to reduce bycatch by decreasing the likelihood of marine animal entanglements with fishing line. This rulemaking is, in part, in response to increased rates of entanglement of humpback whales with Pacific coast fishing gear since 2014. This rule also clarifies requirements regarding the position of escape panels on pot gear to prevent the escape panel from being on the bottom of the pot and to promote consistency across the escape panel requirements for Federal groundfish pot fisheries off Alaska and the three West Coast states. This rulemaking also clarifies bottom longline regulations throughout
50 CFR part 660
for consistency with Pacific Fishery Management Council (Council) recommendations implemented in this rulemaking.
Pursuant to Magnuson-Stevens Act section 303(c)(2) (
16 U.S.C. 1853(c)(2)
), the Council deemed the regulations in this rulemaking necessary and appropriate to implement these actions in a December 20, 2024, letter from Council Executive Director, Merrick Burden, to Regional Administrator Jennifer Quan. The proposed rule was published on February 2, 2026 (
91 FR 5408
). The public comment period was open through March 9, 2026. This rulemaking implements the Groundfish FMP, consistent with the authority provided in sections 6.6 and 6.10.3 of the Groundfish FMP, for gear restrictions being described in this final rule.
Background
This final rule is based on the Council's final recommendations for gear marking and entanglement risk reduction in the groundfish fishery made at its June 2024 meeting in San Diego, CA. In developing the recommended measures, the Council considered the results of a 2022 workshop with the groundfish fishing industry, “Improving Gear Marking in the U.S. West Coast Sablefish Pot Fishery,” as well as reports from its advisory bodies and public testimony. In spring 2026, NMFS considered public comments on the proposed rule and advice from the Council's enforcement consultants in developing this final rule.
The Needs and Scope of This Rulemaking
Marine animals, like whales and turtles, can get caught in fishing gear, which can prevent them from eating or cause serious injury or death. The animal most often entangled in gear associated with the Pacific Coast groundfish fishery is the humpback whale.
This rulemaking removes the regulatory requirement to use surface gear at both ends of groundfish pot and bottom longline gear sets, allowing vessels to reduce the number of vertical lines in the water. This voluntary measure is expected to reduce the
(
printed page 64792)
likelihood of entanglements. This rulemaking is also expected to help NMFS track the source of entanglements by requiring gear-specific marking on two types of commercial “fixed gear” used for catching groundfish off the coasts of Washington, Oregon, and California: (1) pot gear; and (2) bottom longline gear.
Groundfish pot gear (both traditional and slinky pot) uses a series of pots connected by a rope (groundline) on the seafloor. A vertical line and a surface buoy mark the gear's location. Pot gear may sit unattended for 1.5 to up to 7 days, generally a longer period than for bottom longline gear (2 to 48 hours). Because pot gear is heavier than bottom longline gear, it may pose a higher risk of serious injury if an animal becomes entangled.
Bottom longline gear is a horizontal rope (or groundline) with many hooks that lies along the bottom of the sea floor, also marked by vertical lines and surface buoys. It soaks for a shorter time, usually 2 to 48 hours, but may sit unattended for up to 7 days. Groundline for bottom longline gear poses entanglement risk when marine mammals attempt to eat hooked fish.
Entanglement can happen with these fixed gears on the surface with surface lines or surface buoys/markers, in the water column with vertical lines, or at/near the seafloor with the groundline or pots/hooks. Entanglements can also happen with any component as the gear is being hauled to the surface and retrieved. These pot and bottom longline groundfish gears, when fished in Federal waters, are the only gear types affected by this rulemaking. These two gear types, when used to harvest groundfish, are hereafter collectively referred to as the “subject gears” or the “subject gear types.” This rulemaking does not change the requirement that the subject gear types be attended at sea at least every 7 days.
Gear Marking
This rulemaking implements new requirements in the Pacific Coast groundfish fishery for marking all buoys and the top 20 fathoms (fm) (120 feet (ft) or 37 meters (m)) of the vertical line used with the subject gears. For the first 3 years after the initial effective date of these requirements, temporary marking methods may be used to satisfy the line marking requirements, and thereafter the top 20 fm (37 m) of vertical line must be line manufactured in the designated color schemes. NMFS is implementing two color-coded schemes for the new gear marking requirements for the subject gears, as recommended by the Council: one for groundfish pot gear and one for groundfish bottom longline gear.
Table 1—Two-Color Marking Schemes for Bottom Longline and Pot Gears

New Requirements for Marking Buoys
NMFS is implementing a new requirement for either gear-specific buoy tags to be attached to each surface buoy, or gear-specific marks to be made directly on each buoy. Tag and buoy markings are “GP” for pot and “GL” for bottom longline. Vessel identification information must be on at least one buoy, per current regulations, but is also required by this rulemaking to be marked on all other buoys used for the subject gear types, either on the tag or directly on the buoy. Markings are required on every buoy because it is possible that not all buoys would remain connected if the surface gear were to become entangled.
Each tag must have a physical indentation and a contrasting color. Buoy tags on every surface buoy must be in a gear-specific color (table 1), with a gear-specific letter combination legibly marked on it. Tags must be attached to fishing gear when deployed and must be on board the vessel on a trip where groundfish pot or longline gear will be or has been used to take and retain groundfish.
Gear-specific marks directly on buoys must be in capital letters at least 3 inches (7.7 cm) in height and must be present at all times on a trip in which the vessel is taking and retaining groundfish with the subject gears, if gear marking tags are not on board.
In the proposed rule, NMFS proposed that the new buoy marking requirements would require tags attached to each and every surface buoy with a gear-specific color and engraved mark: capital letters “P” for pots and “L” for bottom longline. Buoy tags were proposed because they can be swapped out, which would allow a surface gear set up, including the large buoys used with groundfish gear, to be used to float different gear types. In this final rule, NMFS is requiring that pot and bottom longline gear buoys are marked either by using buoy tags, as proposed, or through gear-specific marks directly on the buoys in response to public comments.
As described below in the Comments and Responses section, one fisherman submitted comments on the proposed rule asking that vessel operators be allowed the option for permanent fishery and gear-specific marks on the buoys that are used to mark surface gear, in lieu of buoy tags, because this option would be more efficient for certain operators and require less maintenance than the proposed gear-specific buoy tags. The State of California requires lobster pots to have buoys marked with a “P.” NMFS considered the request in development of this final rule, and this final rule implements the option to allow for buoy marking using tags or directly on buoys. This final rule also includes a requirement that the buoy marking include a fishery-specific mark as well as a gear-specific mark. These fishery and gear-specific markings must be “GP” for pot and “GL” for longline. See Changes from the Proposed Rule for additional details.
NMFS notes that current regulations require that all fixed groundfish gears, including the subject gears, have at least one buoy with the vessel identification legibly marked on it, per current regulations at
50 CFR 660.219
and
660.319
. This requirement is not revised with this rulemaking.
New Requirements for Marking Lines
This rulemaking requires two-color, gear-specific color schemes for marking the top 20 fm (37 m) of each vertical line deployed in the commercial, non-tribal, limited entry and directed open access groundfish fishery for vessels using pot or bottom longline gears. Lines must be marked in the specified colors by the manufacturer, with strands in each color, except that temporary methods of marking (with the same color scheme) is allowed for 3 years after the effective date of the final rule.
(
printed page 64793)
With this rulemaking, NMFS requires that at least the top 20 fm (37 m) of vertical line be continuously marked. Manufactured line must consist primarily of only the two gear-specific colors A and B specified in table 1. Both colors must be used. NMFS requires that at least one-third of the strands in the rope be one color and all the other strands be the other color required in the gear-specific two-color scheme. Presence of a third color, other than white, is prohibited in the top 20 fm (37 m) to reduce the likelihood of mistaken gear identification for gear that is observed entangled on marine animals. NMFS acknowledges that some types of manufactured line may have an inner core color that is necessary and shows through on the outer surface of the line (
i.e.,
a tracer). This core is usually white. Manufactured line can be ordered by the coil; a standard coil has a line length of 1,200 ft (365.8 m) and costs approximately $200-$500, with custom colors available at no additional cost. Some manufacturers offer different size coils. Manufactured line may be used to satisfy the marking requirements for groundfish pot and bottom longline gears immediately upon the effective date of a final rule.
NMFS expects that the most efficient option for complying with new line marking requirements will be manufactured line in the specified color schemes. Manufactured line is expected to have the greatest longevity. However, some operators may have difficulties in initially procuring manufactured line. Thus, to afford fishery participants sufficient flexibility, and to achieve timely compliance with the line marking requirements in this final rule, this rulemaking includes the allowance to use temporary marking of existing lines for 3 years after this rule's effective date. Any temporary marking scheme requires continuous, alternating bands of the color schemes for each gear type on at least the top 20 fm (37 m) of every vertical line. Alternating marks must consist of colored rope sections that result in a continuous, alternating two-color scheme for each groundfish fixed gear type, as detailed in table 1 above. Each colored band for temporary marks is required to be greater than 18 inches and up to 28 inches (46-71 centimeters (cm)) of linear rope length. Presence of any color rope, besides white, other than the color scheme shown in table 1 in the top 20 fm (37 m) of the vertical line is prohibited for vessels fishing for groundfish with the subject gear types. In order to give fishery operators flexibility in complying with this requirement, NMFS is not specifying a method or material for applying temporary marks in the first 3 years after this final rule is effective. In the development of this action, the Council discussed multiple ways to temporarily achieve the required marking scheme for vertical lines, such as paint (sprayed or dipped) or colored tape. NMFS expects temporary marks will have a lower immediate materials cost than manufactured line but may require more time for maintenance. NMFS is implementing this flexibility in this rulemaking, as recommended by the Council.
Summary of Gear Marking Requirements
The gear marking requirements implemented through this final rule apply to vessels fishing in the limited entry or directed open access groundfish fisheries with bottom longline or pot gear. This final rule requires vessels using the subject fishing gears to comply with the following gear-specific marking schemes (summarized in table 2).
All buoys deployed on limited entry or directed open access groundfish pot surface gear must have either: (1) gear-specific orange tags attached with capital letters “GP” engraved on both sides and the letters must be in a contrasting color; or (2) capital letters “GP” permanently marked directly on the buoy in a contrasting color and at least 3 inches (7.7 cm) in height. The vessel identification number must be included on all buoy tags or directly on all buoys. All markings must be maintained to be legible on an ongoing basis.
All buoys deployed on limited entry or directed open access groundfish bottom longline surface gear must have either: (1) gear-specific brown tags attached with capital letters “GL” engraved on both sides and the letters must be in a contrasting color; or (2) capital letters “GL” permanently marked directly on the buoy in a contrasting color and at least 3 inches (7.7 cm) in height. The vessel identification number must be included on all buoy tags or directly on all buoys. All markings must be maintained to be legible on an ongoing basis.
At least the top 20 fm (37 m) of vertical line used to deploy bottom longline or pot gear in the limited entry or directed open access fishery must be continuously marked in the appropriate gear-specific color scheme. Bottom longline vertical lines are required to be continuously marked in brown and blue. Pot gear vertical lines are required to be continuously marked in orange and blue. Both colors must be used; manufactured lines must be at least one-third of strands in one color and all remaining strands in the other color, with any other color besides white prohibited in the top 20 fm (37 m). Temporarily marked lines are required to be gear-specific, two-color alternating, in continuous bands between 18 and 28 inches (46 and 71 cm) each for a minimum of 20 fm (37 m) at the top of every vertical line.
NMFS is requiring that manufactured line, and only manufactured line, be used to mark vertical lines for the subject gears, beginning January 11, 2030. After that date, temporary markings will no longer satisfy line marking requirements.
