Entanglement Risk Reduction
This section describes voluntary and required management measures that are being implemented with the goal of reducing the risk of entanglement of protected species and bycatch in the subject gear types. These measures affect the same groups of fishermen subject to gear marking requirements described above that use bottom longline or pot gear in directed groundfish fisheries off the West Coast.
Fishing lines on or near the surface generally pose a higher risk of entanglement compared to fishing gear at deeper depths or on the bottom of the sea floor. Therefore, the measures implemented through this rulemaking are designed to reduce the amount of vertical lines required in the fishery and reduce the amount of surface line allowed for each gear set. NMFS expects these measures will reduce the risk of entanglement with surface and vertical lines in Pacific Coast groundfish pot and bottom longline gears.
Single Line Allowance for Gear Identification at the Surface
As noted above, vertical lines and surface gear both pose a risk of entanglement to protected species. Therefore, allowing vessels to reduce the amount of surface gear and the number of lines in the water may reduce risk of entanglement. This rulemaking removes the requirement that pot and bottom longline gear be marked on the surface at both terminal ends (
i.e.,
creates a single surface gear and vertical line allowance). This voluntary measure allows vessel operators to use a vertical line and surface gear at one or both ends of their gear, at their own discretion. Gear would still be required to be marked at the surface on at least one terminal end in a manner consistent with the current gear identification and marking requirements. This single surface gear and vertical line allowance and the manner in which the subject gears must be marked at the surface are articulated in revised regulations at
50 CFR 660.219
and
660.319
.
Limiting Surface Line
Surface gear consists of the buoys and flags associated with a gear set and the surface line between them. Surface gear marks the location of the terminal end(s) of the groundline anchoring the strings of pots and bottom longline gear set on the ocean floor and usually serves as the primary mechanism for identifying and retrieving gear. Surface lines need to have enough slack to adjust to changes in ocean conditions that may occur while gear remains in the water so that the buoys are not submerged completely.
This final rule restricts the maximum length of surface line, measured from the last trailing buoy (or the highflyer) to the first buoy (main buoy) closest to the vertical line. Specifically, surface line used for the subject gears may not exceed 60 ft (10 fm (18 m)) in length, measured from the main buoy to the last trailing buoy. By prohibiting excess surface line, this rulemaking intends to reduce the risk of entanglement and the bycatch of protected species in the groundfish fishery with the subject gears. To enact this restriction, new definitions of surface line, vertical line, and main buoy are added to the definition of “Fishing gear” for the subject gear types at
50 CFR 660.11
.
Additional Regulation Changes
Beyond the gear marking and risk reduction measures described above, this rulemaking also includes two additional changes (see the Proposed Rule for additional context and rationale for these changes). Current regulations require that pot and trap gears are fitted with an escape panel that biodegrades to create an opening of specified dimensions so that the pot does not perpetually entrap animals if the gear is lost (660.230(b) and 660.330(b)). Current regulations provide no specificity about the appropriate placement of the escape panel. This rulemaking prohibits escape panels from being positioned on the bottom of a pot, similar to regulations for fishing off the coast of Alaska and includes an exception from this requirement for collapsible pots in order to accommodate differences in gear
(
printed page 64795)
configurations. To facilitate this collapsible pot exception, a definition of “collapsible pot” is added to the definition of “Fishing gear” at
50 CFR 660.11
.
Additionally, this rulemaking changes the maximum twine size for the cotton biodegradable twine used for closing escape panels for pots used in the Pacific Coast groundfish fishery. Specifically, this rulemaking revises the maximum untreated cotton twine size for closing escape panels from “not to exceed number 21” to “not to exceed number 30.” This modification aligns the maximum twine size for groundfish pot gear used in the Pacific Coast groundfish fishery with the twine size required for vessels fishing off the coast of Alaska (
i.e.,
the North Pacific).
NMFS is making technical changes to
50 CFR part 660
to revise references in the relevant regulations to longline and bottom longline gears to clarify key gear terminology, so that it is clear what type of longline gear is affected by this rulemaking. This rulemaking replaces “longline” with “bottom longline” in the definition of “fixed gear” at
50 CFR 660.11
, and throughout limited entry and open access commercial groundfish regulations, where applicable.
This rulemaking also amends the current prohibition at
50 CFR 660.12(a)(2)
about falsifying or failing to affix or maintain gear markings required under the regulations by adding the word “identifications” to revise the text to align with the current section titles for the regulations referenced in the prohibition (
50 CFR 660.219
and
660.319
), which are, respectively “fixed gear identification and marking” and “open access fishery gear identification and marking.”
Comments and Responses
The proposed rule was published on February 6, 2026 (
91 FR 5408
), and the public comment period ended on March 9, 2026. NMFS received comment letters from 28 individuals or organizations. The following themes were raised across individual submissions. NMFS received comment letters from five commenters expressing general opposition to the proposed measures in this rulemaking, of which three letters specifically described concerns with gear loss related to the measure that would remove the requirement that groundfish bottom longline or pot gear sets be marked with vertical lines and surface gear at both terminal ends (referred to henceforth as “the single-line allowance”). Of the five comment letters generally in opposition to the rule, three of those letters expressed general support for the gear marking and surface line length restrictions in this rule and their objective to indirectly conserve marine mammals. However, commenters also expressed concern with the single-line allowance, asserting that the allowance would increase the risk of gear loss. NMFS received 13 comment letters that were generally in support of this rulemaking. Seven of these letters supported the bycatch reduction measures in this rulemaking but also expressed support for additional measures to conserve marine animals, above and beyond those proposed in this rulemaking. Of the 28 comment letters, 1 letter included comments regarding the PRA collection, which is responded to below and in the PRA supporting statement. Overall, most comments generally expressed support for this rulemaking.
NMFS appreciates the thoughtful comments on the proposed rule and has considered them thoroughly. NMFS collated the comments in the 28 letters, and is responding to 20 subject areas included across the unique comment letters below.
Comment 1:
Two commenters opposed this rulemaking, describing it as unnecessary, and asserting that entanglements of marine animals in fishing gear are rare and are not a consequential conservation issue.
Response:
Entanglements involving commercial fishing gear are estimated based on best scientific information available, and the gears that are the subject of this rulemaking have had multiple documented entanglements with marine animals. NMFS acknowledges that these observed and otherwise documented entanglements in groundfish fixed gear are relatively rare; however, documented entanglements of marine animals in fishing gear of unknown origin is not infrequent and should also be considered. The new requirements in this rule balance the need for reasonable steps forward toward reducing the risk of entanglements with the subject gears and better attributing entanglements in general to the gear-type, with a small additional cost and operational burden on fishermen.
Comment 2:
Two commenters express concern with over-regulation of fisheries and assert that the measures in this rulemaking are unnecessarily burdensome to the regulated fishermen. One of these commenters also states that this rule will increase gear expenses and wear and tear on gear, and that fishermen should be financially compensated for the burden of complying with the measures implemented through this rulemaking.
Response:
Gear marking measures implemented by this rulemaking are expected to increase the likelihood that NMFS can rule out the groundfish fixed gear fishery as the source of documented entanglements, thus reducing the need for further regulation in the future. However, NMFS acknowledges that the approximately 335 vessels that currently fish groundfish with bottom longline or pot gears will be required to incur costs over the next 3 years to comply with the gear marking measures in this rulemaking. NMFS is obligated under the PRA to annualize burden hours and costs over the initial 3-year period of an approved information collection (gear marking requirements are considered an information collection). Since it is unlikely that any vessel would need to purchase gear compliant with new gear marking regulations more than once in this 3-year period, annualized materials costs are one-third of the estimated total materials cost. The average cost burden for compliance with new gear marking regulations in this rulemaking is estimated to be $809 per respondent (
e.g.,
vessel operator) to temporarily mark and replace their gear once during the three-year period preceding the compliance date for permanently marking fixed gear using manufactured line. This total accounts for the costs of gear-specific marked line, gear-specific marked buoy tags, and paint or markers. NMFS understands from fishery representatives that lines used in the fishery need to be replaced once every 5-10 years, with the actual lifetime of the gear depending on the intensity of use, method of storage, and other variables. To reduce the main source of costs associated with this rulemaking (
i.e.,
gear-specific manufactured marked line in a specified color scheme), line marking is only required for the top 20 fm (37 m) of the vertical line (allowing more sets of gear to be marked per spool of line purchased) and a 3-year transition period is included to allow more cost-effective temporary marking schemes to be used initially in lieu of manufactured line. The goal of this transition period is to allow current vertical lines used in the fishery to be phased out and replaced towards the end of their lifespan with gear-specific manufactured marked lines, avoiding unnecessary waste and defraying costs. This rulemaking is not expected to increase wear and tear on fishing gear beyond what usual use would do. In conclusion, NMFS finds that the cost burden on the regulated community imposed by this rule does not outweigh the conservation benefits from this rule.
(
printed page 64796)
Therefore, NMFS is implementing the proposed gear marking requirements in this rulemaking.
Comment 3:
One commenter expressed concern that oil spills and pollution pose greater threats to marine animal conservation than entanglements in fishing gear, and, therefore, that is where NMFS should focus conservation efforts.
Response:
NMFS does not discount the potential adverse impacts of other environmental conditions, such as oil spills and marine debris, which pose threats to marine animals. However, this action is taken under the authority of the Magnuson-Stevens Act and, as such, its regulatory scope is limited to the effects of federally managed fisheries on marine animals. The primary risk these fisheries pose to non-target marine animals is the potential for entanglement in fishing gear. Accordingly, the measures implemented through this final rule are intended to address this primary risk.
Comment 4:
Two commenters state that the amount of fishing gear used in the West Coast EEZ could or will increase in the future, which could subsequently increase the risk of entanglement in the area. One of these commenters expressed concern that this rulemaking does nothing to mitigate this risk.
Response:
NMFS acknowledges that there are no current restrictions on the total amount of gear sets or number of vertical lines that may be deployed annually in the Pacific Coast groundfish fixed gear fisheries, nor were any proposed at the proposed rule stage. However, a variety of facets of the groundfish fishery management regime coincide to keep the amount of fishing gear deployed in the EEZ annually relatively stable through time. For example, the groundfish sector with the majority of the fixed gear fishing effort, both in harvest volume and quantity of gear deployed (
i.e.,
the limited entry fixed gear (LEFG) sector), is Federally permitted through a limited entry program. These federal permits are transferable, but limit vessel size (and therefore limit harvest capacity), and are of a limited quantity (no new permits have been issued for over 20 years). This closed class limits the amount of gear that can be fished at any one time or in any season. Participants in the directed open access fishery may use any legal gear type, including pots and bottom longline gears, but are incentivized to use non-bottom contact gears (
i.e.,
gear that is not left unattended) because those gears are allowed to be fished in areas that are closed to bottom longline and pot gears. Most vessels fishing with bottom longline and pot gear in the open access fishery are targeting sablefish in deeper waters outside gear-specific area restrictions. The amount of overall effort to harvest sablefish in the open access fishery is also limited by the sector's annual allocation and through inseason trip limit adjustments to keep harvest within that allocation. Meaning, if more vessels fish sablefish, trip limits for these vessels decrease to keep catch of sablefish within the annual sector allocation, which reduces the incentives for new entrants to join the fishery. In this manner, the number of vessels targeting sablefish in the open access fishery (regardless of gear type) is self-mitigating. Thus, all other things being equal, the single-line allowance established in this rulemaking is expected to decrease the total number of vertical lines that would otherwise be fished annually in the EEZ than without it. In addition, the single-line allowance creates the opportunity within the fishery for fishermen to test on-demand buoy lines and systems (
i.e.,
“pop-up gear”), if so desired, without an exempted fishing permit, and using their otherwise conventional and legal pot and bottom longline gear configurations.
Comment 5:
Five commenters expressed concern for gear loss if future fishermen use only one vertical line (
i.e.,
voluntarily use the single-line allowance) when setting their gear. Generally, these commenters expressed concern that gear retrieval would be less likely, especially in circumstances where gear sets moved due to strong currents or became snagged or parted on some portion of line during attempted retrieval. One commenter specifically mentioned that the risk of gear loss would be highest for longline gear. Another asserted that a single-line allowance would reduce the likelihood of gear retrieval by 50 percent.
Response:
The Council considered both a mandatory and voluntary single-line allowance during early scoping of this rulemaking. During scoping, concerns were expressed on multiple fronts. For example, industry representatives were concerned that relatively lighter-weight gear types (such as slinky pots and longline gears) would be much more likely to be lost if only a single-line were used, either voluntarily or if required, and explained that certain conditions and methods of deploying gear did not lend themselves to successful gear retrieval if gear could only be marked on one end (
i.e.,
under a mandatory single-line requirement). Multiple environmental groups expressed concern that a non-mandatory single-line would be ineffectual to reduce the risk of entanglement. All comments were considered by the Council, and the Council ultimately recommended a voluntary single-line allowance for the subject gear types. NMFS has determined that the Council-recommended single-line allowance is appropriate because it will provide the flexibility to allow vessels to mark only one end of their pot or bottom longline gear if fishermen consider ocean conditions exist that are likely to enable full retrieval of the gear using a single vertical line. Some vessels may choose to use heavier single lines to increase the likelihood of preventing their gear from parting during retrieval. Other fishermen may choose to continue to use current gear configurations, with lines and surface gear at both ends, despite the rule change. Regardless, NMFS is confident that fishermen are both strongly disincentivized from losing their gear and from deploying extraneous gear, and will make their future gear use decisions accordingly. NMFS has heard testimony from multiple fishermen that they are likely to utilize the single-line allowance, which will reduce the number of vertical lines in the water. For these reasons, NMFS concludes that the voluntary single-line allowance appropriately balances the need to reduce the risk of entanglement in fishing gear against the need to prevent gear loss and subsequent ghost fishing.
Comment 6:
Two commenters expressed concern with the limitation on the length of surface line associated with the terminal end of a gear set that is implemented in this rulemaking. The limitation is intended to reduce the amount of slack or excess surface line that attaches buoys to the vertical line. One commenter was concerned that the length limit of the surface line was too short and would result, under certain ocean conditions, in the gear fully submerging in the tide and therefore being lost. The other commenter expressed concern that the limit on the length of the surface line was too long to sufficiently eliminate the risk of entanglement.
Response:
These comments exemplify the purpose of this measure: to keep fishing gear viable and retrievable while limiting excess line to try to reduce the risk of entanglements. In developing this measure, the Council heard from fishing industry representatives that, in their experience, 10 fm (18.3 m) or less of surface line would be an adequate length to prevent the gear from being submerged in most ocean conditions. NMFS acknowledges that allowing any fishing with fixed gears poses a greater than zero risk of entanglement,
(
printed page 64797)
regardless of the length of surface line. The goal of this rulemaking is to reduce the risk of entanglement. NMFS has determined that the surface line limitation of 10 fm (18.3 m) is the appropriate length for the surface line limitation to balance the need to reduce the risk of entanglement, and thus minimize the bycatch of marine animals with the subject gears, against the threat of gear submergence and loss.
Comment 7:
Ten comment letters explicitly expressed support for NMFS to protect marine mammals and reduce bycatch and/or risk of entanglement for various marine species, either generally (without a reference to the measures in this rulemaking) or as it relates to measures in this rulemaking (
e.g.,
the single-line allowance). Of these 10 letters, 7 letters expressed general support for greater protections for marine animals. However, only one of those 7 letters explicitly expressed support for the proposed measures. Though most of the 10 comments did not explicitly reference the measures in this rulemaking, it is inferred that comments asking for the strongest measures possible to protect marine mammals express concern that the proposed measures do not offer enough protection. Of the 7 comment letters requesting greater protections, 4 expressed general support for actions that would reduce lines in the water as means to achieve risk reduction, though none explicitly endorsed the single-line allowance. One letter mentioned a desire to “create less fishing lines” in the ocean, thought it was unclear whether this was an endorsement of the single-line allowance or not. One letter explicitly commented that the voluntary single-line allowance is inadequate because it was possible that, even if fishermen used one end-line, they may deploy shorter but more numerous gear sets, meaning the number of vertical lines per pot fished would stay the same.
Response:
NMFS agrees that it is important to reduce the risk of entanglement and bycatch of marine mammals in fisheries and fishing gear. This goal is an important component of NMFS' obligations under the Magnuson-Stevens Act and pursuant to other applicable laws, such as the Endangered Species Act (ESA) and the Marine Mammal Protection Act (MMPA). Minimizing bycatch to the extent practicable is a necessary part of fisheries management under the Magnuson-Stevens Act, and this action is consistent with that mandate. This rulemaking began as a response to increased entanglements on the West Coast in 2014. This rulemaking will remove a regulatory barrier that currently prohibits fishermen from deploying fewer fishing lines. As discussed in
Response to Comment 5,
NMFS is confident that fishermen are strongly disincentivized from deploying extraneous gear and from losing gear. This rulemaking allows the flexibility for fishermen to decide and deploy their gear configurations to best balance these needs, based on ocean conditions. Because marking gear with only one end-line is voluntary, there is no specific incentive created by this rulemaking for fishermen to shift towards fewer pots per set. Finally, NMFS intends to collect data on the use of the voluntary single-line allowance via Federal observers and self-reported logbook entries. This will further inform future considerations regarding the efficacy of, and possible future adjustments to, the voluntary measure implemented in this rulemaking.
Comment 8:
Two commenters suggested that NMFS make the single-line allowance mandatory instead of voluntary, one of whom asserts that the reduction in risk of entanglements is negligible if the single-line allowance in this rulemaking is voluntary because fishermen may not use only a single end-line.
Response:
A requirement for marking only one end of gear (
i.e.,
a mandatory single-line) at the surface was considered, but not recommended, by the Council. See also
Response to Comment 5
and
Response to Comment 7,
which are incorporated here. Groundfish are harvested at a variety of depths, but sablefish are abundant and commonly harvested with the subject gear types at depths of 600 fm (3,600 ft) and deeper. The effects of tidal swells, strong currents, and windy conditions are considerable at these depths and can cause the surface gear, which is used by a vessel to retrieve its gear, to become fully submerged at times. If submerged deep enough, or long enough, buoys may deflate and no longer mark the gear at the surface, even when conditions become more favorable. In these conditions, if regulations required only one set of surface gear to be used, it would most certainly increase the likelihood of gear loss, or ocean conditions would effectively close the fishery at those depths while such ocean conditions persist. Gear that is not successfully retrieved can continue to harvest fish (
i.e.,
ghost fishing) and pose a continued risk of entanglement. Gear requirements that are reasonably expected to increase gear loss are not consistent with the Magnuson-Stevens Act mandates regarding minimizing bycatch to the extent practicable, and, as such, the Council did not recommend that NMFS adopt a mandatory single-line requirement. For these reasons, and the reasons stated in
Response to Comment 5
and
Response to Comment 7,
NMFS has determined that the voluntary single-line allowance fishery management measure to minimize bycatch is consistent with the Magnuson-Stevens Act and other applicable laws, including the ESA and MMPA.
Comment 9:
One commenter asked for NMFS to limit fishing in cetacean hotspots (
e.g.,
enact closed areas) to reduce and prevent the entanglement of marine species.
Response:
NMFS considered available information on timing and location of entanglements in groundfish bottom longline and pot gears during the development of this rulemaking. Given the relative rarity of entanglements in groundfish gear, and the lack of readily available information on the spatial or seasonal patterns for groundfish gear entanglements and for predicting the likely overlap of marine mammals and the groundfish fishery in space and time, the Council did not develop alternatives for this action that involved area closures (
e.g.,
permanent or seasonal). NMFS expects that the gear marking provisions in this rulemaking are likely to provide new information on entanglements that may inform the development of future conservation measures, as needed.
Comment 10:
One commenter noted that the single-line allowance would likely provide the most entanglement risk reduction for gears that are left in the water to “soak” longer (
i.e.,
pot gear). This fisherman asked for NMFS to consider soak times when deciding whether to provide the single-line allowance to either longline or pot gears, or both, describing that if they tried to use a single-line with their bottom longline gear they might lose tens of thousands of dollars' worth of gear.
Response:
NMFS' groundfish regulations require that all fixed gear (
e.g.,
bottom longline, pot) used in the groundfish fishery be tended once at least every 7 days. Beyond this requirement, which is intended to discourage storage of fishing gear at-sea, there are no rules regarding minimum or maximum soak times; it is at the fisherman's discretion. In the report for the “Improving Gear Marking in the U.S. West Coast Sablefish Pot Fleet; Workshop Summary Report, November 16, 2022,” published by Oregon Sea Grant, one sablefish pot fishermen testified that they soak their gear for 36 hours on average (but will sometimes
(
printed page 64798)
soak for 3 days and occasionally up to 5 days) between trips, because pots are highly selective and trap fish more slowly than hooks. The amount of time that fixed gear soaks in the water affects the entanglement risk associated with that gear, particularly if gear is marked at both ends. Based on this very limited sample, because pot gear tends to be in the water longer, it follows logic that if pots use the single-line allowance, it would be a bigger reduction in the hours that vertical lines are in the water than if a bottom longline were to use a single-line. During Council testimony, multiple pot fishermen testified that they would be very likely to use the single-line allowance in favorable ocean conditions, because of the gear configurations they use that prevent gear loss. The Council did not consider offering a single-line allowance only to pot fishermen. To reduce regulatory complexity, the single-line allowance applies to both bottom longline and pot gears, though NMFS acknowledges that fishermen fishing bottom longline gear may not utilize this flexibility due to concerns of losing their gear.
Comment 11:
One commenter strongly suggested that NMFS approve the voluntary single-line allowance because it would, “dramatically improve our productivity while greatly reducing entanglement risk to wildlife.”
Response:
NMFS agrees that allowing fishermen to voluntarily use one vertical line to mark their gear at the surface could reduce costs for unnecessary gear, reduce the number of vertical lines deployed in the fishery, and reduce risk of entanglement for marine animals. For these reasons, NMFS is approving this Council-recommended management measure.
Comment 12:
One commenter only offered support for the marking of lines so entanglements can be properly attributed to the fishery it occurs in. Another commenter stated that the proposed measures would improve accountability for the harm caused to wildlife.
Response:
NMFS agrees that the gear marking measures in this rulemaking are an important step in a larger effort across West Coast fisheries to improve our ability to attribute entanglements of unknown sources to particular fisheries, so that management responses can be effective at reducing entanglements without being overly burdensome.
Comment 13:
Nine commenters explicitly supported all the gear marking and entanglement risk reduction measures in this rulemaking, expressing gratitude for consulting with fishermen, reducing marine mammal entanglements through science-based decision making, and for practical, fishery-specific management approaches. NMFS notes that one of these seven commenters expressed support for the proposed measures only as a first step, stating that more conservation measures are needed (see
Comment 7
).
Response:
NMFS appreciates these comments and notes that additional conservation measures are outside the scope of this rulemaking (see also
Response to Comment 7
).
Comment 14:
Two commenters asked NMFS to monitor the efficacy of the measures implemented in this rulemaking, including whether marking requirements after the 3-year temporary marking transition period are working as intended, and whether entanglement rates decline.
Response:
NMFS will continue to monitor entanglements of marine animals off the West Coast and continue to try to attribute them to identifiable sources. NMFS will take into account gear marking requirements in various West Coast fisheries, including the requirements established under this rule, when attempting to attribute an entanglement to its source. NMFS publishes entanglement reports annually and analyzes data for trends and other factors of concern. NMFS will also continue to enforce, in partnership with state offices, Federal fishing regulations, including measures implemented in this rulemaking.
Comment 15:
One commenter asked NMFS to provide guidance with regards to line marking requirements, including temporary marking. They asked how to account for gaps, knots, wear, or the use of non-solid “tracer” lines. Also, they requested further guidance on acceptable temporary marking methods and what NMFS means by “continuous.” With this guidance, they hope to reduce compliance uncertainty and enforcement inconsistency.
Response:
NMFS agrees that steps should be taken to reduce compliance uncertainty and enforcement inconsistency. NMFS offers the following clarifications to facilitate consistent enforcement of gear marking requirements promulgated in this rulemaking, in addition to forthcoming informational guides.
The gear marking requirements implemented through this final rule apply to vessels fishing groundfish in the commercial, non-tribal, limited entry or directed open access fisheries using bottom longline or pot gear.
With regards to buoy marking, before leaving port on a trip where gear marking requirements apply, the vessel is required to have either enough buoy tags of the required color and marking to mark all applicable gear(s) on board the vessel, or all buoys must have compliant gear-specific markings directly on the buoys. Every buoy used to mark bottom longline or pot gear must have legible vessel identification, directly marked on the surface of at least one buoy on every set, and either directly on all other buoys or on marked tags ready to be attached for all other buoys. Buoys on board that are clearly marked for fishing in non-groundfish fisheries (
e.g.,
pot gears marked for fishing spiny lobster) are not subject to groundfish gear marking requirements implemented in this rulemaking.
With regards to line marking, before leaving port on a trip where gear marking requirements apply, the vessel is required to have a sufficient length of marked line to mark at least the top 20 fm (37 m) of all vertical lines to be deployed on each set. Line is considered “marked” when it is manufactured in the applicable two-color scheme found in table 1, with at least one-third of strands being in one color and the remainder being in the other color. Presence of a third color, besides white, is prohibited in the top 20 fm (37 m) to reduce the likelihood of mistaken gear identification for gear that is observed entangled on marine animals. NMFS acknowledges that some types of manufactured line may have an un-customizable inner core color that shows through on the outer surface of the line (
i.e.,
a tracer). This core is usually white. Tracers that are not solid white will be found in non-compliance with line marking requirements. Until January 11, 2030, line is considered “marked” when original line is temporarily marked continuously in the applicable two-color scheme found in table 1, with alternating bands of color, for at least the top 20 fm (37 m) of every vertical line deployed with the subject gears. In the context of temporary line marking, “continuous” means marking is uninterrupted two-color (table 1) alternating bands of markings in the top 20 fm (37 m) of line, with the exception that the original line may be partially visible for less than 6 inches and not at all visible in the full circumference of the temporarily marked portion of the line. Markings that are partially worn (
i.e.,
discolored or missing such that original line color shows through) on one or more sides of the line for a distance greater than 6 inches (15.2 cm) are not “continuous” and do not satisfy line marking requirements. Additionally, any amount of original line showing in the full circumference of the line is not “continuous” and
(
printed page 64799)
therefore does not satisfy line marking requirements. NMFS does not prescribe temporary marking methods, only the outcome: 20 fm (37 m) of continuous marking in the required length intervals and color scheme.
Comment 16:
Two commenters asked NMFS to expand line marking requirements beyond the top 20 fm (37 m) of the vertical line, to include surface lines, the entire vertical line, and all groundlines. Both commenters argue that the only option that allows NMFS to determine with certainty that an entanglement is caused by certain gear (in this case, groundfish pot or bottom longline gear) and, conversely, rule out groundfish pot or bottom longline gear when it is not involved, is by requiring the proposed marking schemes for all parts of the gear. Both commenters argued that because only a small portion of gear (less than 20 ft but often less than 5 ft) is observed entangled, marking 20 fm out of hundreds of fathoms of line is inadequate to ensure entangled gear is identified as groundfish pot or longline gear. They assert that if only part of the gear is marked, entanglements may not be attributed to the groundfish bottom longline and pot gear fishery only because not all parts of the gear are marked. One commenter asserts that NMFS' desire to minimize costs cannot outweigh evidence that marking such a small portion of the gear will fail in many instances to allow NMFS to determine with certainty whether groundfish pot or longline gear is involved in an entanglement. The other of the two commenters argued that an observed entanglement in a sablefish pot groundline warrants additional marking of groundlines and that anything less than marking all parts of gear would be ineffective to definitively attribute entangled gear to a specific fishery.
Response:
As reported at the 2022 Gear Marking Workshop, a groundfish pot gear fishermen described fishing in depths of up to 900 fm (137 m), using strings of pot gear (
i.e.,
sets) up to 1.5 miles (2.4 km) long. During the workshop, a groundfish pot gear fishermen commented that, when fishing so deep and with the influence of ocean currents, their vertical lines might each be up to 1,200 fm (2,195 m) long to allow successful gear retrieval. When up to 10 fm (18 m) of surface gear is attached to the top of the vertical line, this results in a single set of gear, even using the single-line allowance, that could have lines totaling up to 2,580 fm (4,718 m) in length. Spools of custom-colored braided poly cord (
i.e.,
line) are typically 200 fm (366 m) long and cost approximately $500 each. If gear marking were required for all parts of the gear, each set could take up to 13 coils of line to retrofit, at a cost of up to $6,500 per set. Fishermen vary in how many sets they fish, but it is often 2 to 7 sets per trip. For a vessel that fishes more gear, retrofitting seven sets of groundfish pot gear entirely with manufactured lines in the required gear-specific color scheme could cost over $45,000 in materials alone.
The cost of replacing worn-out gear is a known and budgeted fishing expense for most vessel operators and fishing businesses. It is likely that they would commonly budget to replace line on a small proportion of their gear each year and on an as needed basis. As discussed at the Gear Marking Workshop in 2022, the larger proportion of gear that is required to be marked, the greater the costs to the industry to comply. Industry representatives voiced concerns that the initial costs to replace all gear at once could be very expensive and asked for consideration of marking only a portion of their gear (
i.e.,
the parts of their gear that would be most likely to be involved in an entanglement).
As NMFS stated in the 2022 Gear Marking Workshop, based on current entanglement information, line marking on the upper portion of the gear would be most helpful at identifying the source of entanglements. This is because most entanglements involve buoys (
i.e.,
upper or surface portion of fishing gear) or portions of line identified to be from the upper portion of fishing gear. The Council considered various marking distances, including marking surface lines and marking more and less than 20 fm (37 m) on the upper portion of the vertical line. The Council did not recommend gear-specific surface line markings for the same reasons they did not recommend gear-specific markings on buoys: surface lines are commonly used to float different gear types or in different fisheries. The Council recommended the intermediate alternative for the distance of vertical line marking, the top 20 fm (37 m) or 120 ft, because that is the portion of gear most often documented in entanglements, and usually the amount of line in an entanglement is only 6 to 20 ft (2 to 6 m). The Council also recommended this distance because the average-sized groundfish pot fishing operation could mark all their groundfish pot gear (2 to 5 sets) by purchasing a single coil of line for approximately $500, while larger operations may only need to buy two coils of line for approximately $1,000. For these reasons, and for reasons described above in
Response to Comment 13,
NMFS has determined that the measures implemented in this rulemaking minimize bycatch to the extent practicable and are reasonably expected to improve accountability in the groundfish pot and bottom longline fisheries, if entanglements occur in the future, while balancing costs to industry.
Comment 17:
Two commenters state that the measures in this rulemaking are not sufficient to address entanglement concerns and satisfy legal requirements for the West Coast groundfish fishery, nor are they enough to reduce the large proportion of “unknown” entanglements that cannot be attributed to a specific fishery or region, and, therefore, NMFS will be unable to obtain reliable estimates of incidental bycatch.
Response:
This rulemaking, taken under the authority of the Magnuson-Stevens Act, is consistent with NMFS' obligations under the Magnuson-Stevens Act, ESA, MMPA, and other laws. As discussed above, minimizing bycatch to the extent practicable is a necessary part of NMFS' fisheries management. Given the removal of the regulatory requirement to mark gear sets on the surface at both terminal ends (
i.e.,
voluntary single-line allowance), NMFS expects this rulemaking to reduce the number of vertical lines used to identify pot gear in groundfish fisheries, which NMFS expects to reduce the likelihood of entanglements with pot gear. Additionally, given the new limitation on surface line length implemented in this rule, NMFS expects this rulemaking to reduce excess surface line in the water, which NMFS anticipates will reduce the risk of entanglement in both pot and bottom longline gear. The single-line allowance measure in this rule balances minimizing bycatch from entanglements with active fishing gear against the flexibility fishermen need to keep bycatch from ghost fishing gear low. The surface line length limitation balances minimizing excess surface line in the water against the flexibility fishermen need to set gear that can withstand changing ocean conditions and tides, without submergence. Thus, these entanglement risk reduction measures minimize bycatch to the extent practicable, consistent with legal requirements, including the National Standards of the Magnuson-Stevens Act.
Comment 18:
One commenter, referring to a 2012 biological opinion on the groundfish fishery, describes how NMFS thought, at that time, that the observer program would not be able to provide accurate bycatch estimates for entangled humpback whales because
(
printed page 64800)
the gear is left untended and the whales are mobile once entangled in the gear. Based on this, the commenter asserts that the observer program provides an underestimate of actual entanglements occurring in the fishery and that the magnitude of undocumented and unobserved entanglements within the groundfish fishery could be large.
Response:
In 2012, when the referenced biological opinion was completed by NMFS, only one humpback whale had been reported entangled in groundfish fixed gear since 1982, and that entanglement (2006) was not witnessed by a federal observer. Because observer coverage rates of all vessels fishing groundfish pot and longline gears prior to 2011 ranged from 6 to 25 percent annually, averaging 16 percent of targeted landings, NMFS presumed at the time that observer data alone would be insufficient to discern bycatch rates of protected species in the fishery. Beginning in 2011, sablefish have been harvested with non-trawl gear, including the subject gears, under gear switching provisions in the Shorebased Individual Fishing Quota (IFQ) Program (historically quota that was harvested with bottom trawl gear). This IFQ fishing has been observed at much higher rates (approximately 100 percent) than in years prior. From 2011 through 2025, no entanglements were observed in pot or bottom longline gear in this sector. However, during that same period, 4 of the other 6 documented entanglements in groundfish fixed gear were observed (2014, 2016, 2023, and 2025) in non-IFQ sectors of the groundfish fishery. There have also been initial reports of entanglements in groundfish fixed gear during the 2026 fishing season. For example, on July 7, 2026, a deceased humpback whale was observed entangled in groundfish pot gear. Additionally, on July 23, 2026, there was a report of a whale entanglement associated with multiple gear types off the coast of Oregon, including sablefish pot gear. An investigation into the circumstances of these entanglements is ongoing by NMFS scientists and entanglement experts. Further information on the entanglements, and potential implications for future action(s) to address the mortality and serious injury of humpback whales in the sablefish pot fishery, will be discussed by the West Coast Take Reduction Team (TRT). The TRT web page is available at
www.fisheries.noaa.gov
by searching for “west coast take reduction team.”
To date, no entanglement cases have been clearly identified as involving a mobile, free-swimming entanglement involving sablefish pot fishing gear. Since the 2012 biological opinion, NMFS has completed 2 additional consultations and biological opinions addressing humpback whale bycatch in the sablefish pot fishery, including consideration of reported entanglements that have occurred since 2012. Additionally, NMFS has modified the bycatch estimation approach since 2012 to better deal with relatively rare events like humpback whale entanglements in the groundfish fishery and limited observer coverage. NMFS has adopted and utilized methodologies for extrapolating observed entanglements to inform fleet-wide estimates in acknowledgement of limited observer coverage since 2020. Given the weight of updated information, the statement from the 2012 biological opinion is not representative of NMFS' current perspective. NMFS finds that it is unlikely that a whale that becomes entangled in groundfish pot gear will move the gear away from its original location due to the gear's weight and its propensity to anchor whales in place when entanglements have been documented in the past, and that there is an extremely low amount of gear loss documented in the fishery. If mobile entanglements occurred, rates of gear loss would be higher. Line marking requirements in this rulemaking will allow NMFS to ground truth this hypothesis.

NMFS is publishing this final rule with a 90-day delay in effectiveness for most provisions in this rulemaking, including the gear marking requirements. NMFS is waiving the delay in effectiveness for the voluntary single-line allowance provisions, at

Comment 20:
One commenter requested specific changes to proposed regulatory text to further increase flexibility on complying with new buoy marking requirements and to simplify and clarify regulatory requirements for the placement of escape panels on pots.
Response:
NMFS finds merit in the suggested regulatory changes and concludes that they constitute a logical outgrowth of the specific requirements described in the proposed rule. See Changes from the Proposed Rule for additional information.
Changes From the Proposed Rule
Additional Buoy Marking Method
Based on public comments, NMFS is adding an additional method for complying with the requirement for gear-specific marks on buoys. Instead of buoy tags being the only method of compliance for the gear-specific buoy marking required, as proposed in the proposed rule, the final rule adds the option for gear-specific marks directly on buoys. This will allow vessel operators that use dedicated, gear-specific surface gear to float either pot or bottom longline gear, exclusively, to permanently and directly mark all buoys. As described in the proposed rule, this method of marking was considered by the Council, but was not recommended because some fishermen testified that they often used surface lines and buoys to float multiple gear types within a fishing vessel's portfolio of target species. For those fishermen, marking directly on buoys was disfavored because it would force the purchase and storage of extra surface gear. However, the Council did not consider allowing multiple methods of buoy marking during development of its recommendation. NMFS finds that expanding the allowable methods for compliance with the gear-specific buoy marking requirements in this rule is appropriate and consistent with the Council's recommendation. Adding this method of marking buoys to the final rule provides operational efficiencies to the fleet, while still achieving the intended goal of gear-specific markings on all pot and bottom longline buoys. As such, this change to the final rule is consistent with NMFS' original purpose for this action and considered a logical outgrowth of the proposed rule. The change neither raises new issues not addressed in, nor represents a substantial departure from the proposed rule. For these reasons, NMFS is revising regulatory text at
50 CFR 660.219(b)(1)
and
660.319(b)(1)
to add an additional method of complying with this rule's buoy marking requirements by marking directly on the buoys, using capital letters “GL” for bottom longline buoys and “GP” for pot buoys.
Additionally, NMFS is making technical revisions to these regulations providing that all buoy markings, whether directly on the buoy or via buoy tag, use the capital letters “GL” for bottom longline buoys/tags and “GP” for pot buoys/tags, rather than the “P” and “L” markings provided in the proposed rule. These technical edits are intended to ensure the fishery-specific and gear-specific buoy marks required for the groundfish fishery under this
(
printed page 64801)
rule are not too similar to buoy markings currently required in other non-groundfish fisheries, including those managed by the State of California. NMFS' revisions to § 660.12(a)(9), as contained in the proposed rule, included gear-specific buoy marking tags as a required component of fishing gear (whether attached to the gear or onboard the vessel) that must be presented to an authorized officer for inspection upon request. In this final rule, gear-specific buoy marking tags are required only if buoys are not directly marked with permanent fishery and gear-specific markings. Therefore, this final rule adds “when required” to the buoy tag inspection requirement at § 660.12(a)(9).
Clarifying Edits to Temporary Line Marking Requirements
Based on public comments, NMFS is adding clarifying text to regulations describing continuous temporary markings for vertical lines in the gear-specific color schemes (table 1). NMFS acknowledges that “continuous” may be open for interpretation, and clarifies specific allowances for original line color showing in the portion of line required to be marked. Line marked in alternating bands of color according to the temporary line marking requirements at § 660.219(b)(2)(ii) and § 660.319(b)(2)(ii) may have up to 6 inches of original line visible, and may not have any original line showing through in the full circumference in the portion of the line required to be marked. See also Response to Comment 15.
Clarifying Edits to Biodegradable Escape Panel Placement Requirements
The proposed rule added specificity in the regulations regarding the required location of the opening of a pot's biodegradable escape panel. The goal of this regulatory change being to ensure that the opening is not on the bottom of the pot or too close to the bottom of the pot to be obstructed by silting or other benthic obstructions. The proposed language was identical to the rules for biodegradable escape panels used in pot fishing off the coast of Alaska. Based on public comments, and after further consultation with regional enforcement agents, NMFS is rewording the requirement at § 660.230(b)(4) and § 660.330 (b)(2)(iii) to simplify the escape panel language and make it slightly less prescriptive by removing the phrase “parallel to,” and to make the intent clearer by stating the escape panel opening must be positioned near but not on the bottom of the pot. The language revisions are consistent with NMFS' original purpose for this regulatory change and neither raise new issues not addressed in, nor represent a substantial departure from the proposed rule action. Thus, these revisions are considered a logical outgrowth of the proposed rule.
Regulations at § 660.219 are revised from the proposed rule to expand the existing gear marking and identification requirements that would have been applicable to only bottom longline and pot gears to apply to all fixed gears authorized for use in the limited entry non-trawl fishery. This change revises the regulations, including language that was not proposed to change in the proposed rule, to bring these provisions into compliance with substantive regulatory amendments that were made in a separate but related rulemaking: the Limited Entry Fixed Gear (LEFG) Follow-On action, for which the final rule published on July 22, 2026 (
91 FR 46000
). The LEFG Follow-On action authorizes more types of fixed gear to be used in the limited entry non-trawl fishery (formerly limited entry fixed gear fishery). This means there are more types of fixed gear that need to have appropriate identification, per existing requirements in § 660.219. These changes are isolated in paragraphs (a)(1) and (a)(2) of § 660.219. The regulations at § 660.219 pertaining to the final gear marking regulation changes implemented by this rulemaking for bottom longline gear and pot gear at (a)(1) and (b) are not substantively changed from the proposed rule, other than the additional buoy marking method described above for pot and bottom longline types of fixed gear.
Surface Line Length Restrictions for the Limited Entry and Open Access Fisheries
The proposed rule included restrictions on the length of surface lines that may be used for bottom longline and pot gear in the limited entry fishery at § 660.230(b)(7). Since the proposed rule, the paragraph numbering in § 660.230(b) has been revised through a separate rulemaking. Accordingly, the surface line length restriction for the limited entry fishery is now published, as proposed, at § 660.230(b)(6) rather than § 660.230(b)(7). This technical correction is made simply to make the regulatory changes implemented through this final rule consistent with the new paragraph numbering in § 660.230(b).
Additionally, the proposed rule for this action mistakenly omitted the surface length restriction for the subject gears that is being implemented in this rulemaking in the open access fishery gear restrictions, which are at § 660.330(b). As described in the preamble to the proposed rule, the intent of the surface line length restriction implemented in this rulemaking was that it would be applicable to all commercial fishing for groundfish on the West Coast using the subject gears, including vessels fishing for groundfish in the open access fishery. Accordingly, the proposed rule's omission of the surface line length restriction in the regulatory text at § 660.330(b) was a mistake and this final rule corrects that mistake by including the new surface line length restriction for vessels fishing with the subject gears in the open access fishery at § 660.330(b)(2)(v). This addition to the regulatory changes implemented through this final rule is consistent with NMFS' original purpose for this action and neither raises new issues not addressed in, nor represents a substantial departure from the purpose and intent for this action as described in the proposed rule. Therefore, this change is considered a logical outgrowth of the proposed rule.

The NMFS Assistant Administrator finds that the requirement for a 30-day delay in the date of effectiveness for select regulations in this rulemaking does not apply pursuant to
5 U.S.C. 553(d)(1)
and
(3)
and makes the regulations implementing the voluntary single-line allowance effective upon publication of this final rule in the
Federal Register
.
Pursuant to
5 U.S.C. 553(d)(1)
, this rule relieves a restriction on fishing because it creates additional flexibility in the amount and type of fishing gear required to be deployed for the subject gears by allowing fixed gear groundfish vessels to voluntarily mark only one terminal end of a pot or bottom longline gear set when a fisherman considers ocean conditions make doing so appropriate. This means that fishermen would be allowed to voluntarily decide to use surface gear (
i.e.,
a pole, flag, light, radar reflector, and a buoy) and a vertical line at only one terminal end of a pot or bottom longline gear set. Fishery participants are currently restricted from deploying the subject gear sets without the sets being marked at the surface on both terminal ends (per current regulations at
50 CFR 660.219(a)(1)
and
660.319(a)(1)
); thus, the voluntary single-line allowance provided for under this final rule will relieve that restriction and, pursuant to
5 U.S.C. 553(d)(1)
, the 30-day delay in effective date requirement does not apply to the regulations implementing the single-line allowance.
Additionally, pursuant to
5 U.S.C. 553(d)(3)
, the 30-day delay in effective date requirement does not apply to the single-line allowance in this final rule because a 30-day delay would be contrary to the public interest as it would delay entanglement risk reduction measures intended to provide conservation benefits to marine animals, particularly humpback whales, by reducing the number of vertical lines required to be deployed in the groundfish fishery during the 2026 fishing year. This provision taking effect without a 30-day delay will benefit the public because it will provide additional flexibilities for fishermen during the 2026 summer harvest of sablefish, which would likely reduce the number of vertical lines deployed, and thus reduce the likelihood of humpback whale and other entanglements, particularly over the summer months when whale presence is highest and overlaps with fishing using the subject gears. As described above in the response to comments, during summer 2026, there have been multiple reported entanglements where initial reports indicate the presence of groundfish gear, including pot gear. Therefore, NMFS feels that it is in the public's interest to promptly implement the single-line allowance to provide fishermen with the flexibility to use only one set of surface gear and vertical lines with the subject gears, and thus to reduce the risk of entanglement, accordingly.
Additionally, NMFS finds it is in the public interest to make the single-line allowance effective upon publication of this rule in the
Federal Register
because the gear flexibility created by the single-line allowance is expected to increase efficiency within the fishery by reducing the amount of fishing gear required when using the subject gear types. The sooner fishery participants are allowed to use this flexibility during the 2026 season, the sooner the economic benefits of these efficiencies can be realized for fishery participants and fishing communities.
Finally, a 30-day delay in effective date is not necessary to provide sufficient notice to the fishing community to adjust to the single-line allowance. One of the general policy purposes for allowing for a delay in a rule's effectiveness is to give the regulated community time to adjust their practices to come into compliance with the requirements of a new rule. The voluntary single-line allowance promulgated in this final rule creates no new compliance burdens for the fishing community affected by this rule. Instead, the rule creates increased operational flexibility on the part of fishery participants. Therefore, there are no policy reasons to delay the effectiveness of the single-line allowance.
For the foregoing reasons, the 30-day delay in the effectiveness pursuant to
5 U.S.C. 553(d)(1)
and
(3)
does not apply to the single-line allowance established at
50 CFR 660.219(a)(1)
and
660.319(a)(1)
and these provisions will be effective immediately upon the publication of this rule in the
Federal Register
.

Regulatory Flexibility Act (RFA)
A final regulatory flexibility analysis (FRFA) was prepared, as required by section 603 of the RFA. The FRFA describes the economic impact this rulemaking will have on small entities. A description of the action, why it is being considered, and the legal basis for this action are contained at the beginning of this section in the preamble and in the
SUMMARY
section of the preamble. A summary of the analysis follows. A copy of this analysis is available from NMFS (see
ADDRESSES
).
For purposes of the RFA (
5 U.S.C. 601
et seq.
) only, NMFS has established a small business size standard for businesses, including their affiliates, whose primary industry is commercial fishing (see
50 CFR 200.2
). A business primarily engaged in commercial fishing is classified as a small business if it is independently owned and operated, is not dominant in its field of operation (including its affiliates), and has combined annual receipts not in excess of $11 million for all its affiliated operations worldwide. This standard applies to all businesses classified under North American Industry Classification System (NAICS) code 11411 for commercial fishing, including all businesses classified as commercial finfish fishing (NAICS 114111), commercial shellfish fishing (NAICS 114112), and other commercial marine fishing (NAICS 114119) businesses (
50 CFR 200.2
;
13 CFR 121.201
).
All commercial groundfish participants that use bottom longline or pot gears in the limited entry or directed open access fisheries in the EEZ off the West Coast, which are managed under the Groundfish FMP, may be affected by this rulemaking. The gear marking and entanglement risk reduction measures require the specified gear marking and surface line limitation described in this final rule for non-Tribal commercial vessels deploying either gear type. Examples of gears that are not affected by this rulemaking include select non-trawl gear types (
i.e.,
troll gear and commercial vertical hook-and-line gear not anchored to the bottom, such as vertical jig gear or rod-and-reel gear with weights suspended off the bottom).
This final rule is needed to increase NMFS' ability to attribute protected species entanglements to specific fisheries and ultimately aid in understanding and reducing the risk of protected species entanglement in groundfish pot and longline gear. The gear marking and entanglement risk reductions in this rule are expected to improve NMFS' ability to attribute the source of protected species entanglements. This rulemaking is also needed to improve the effectiveness of the currently required biodegradable
(
printed page 64803)
escape mechanisms in pot gear. Regulations describing in greater detail the location of escape panels in pot gear is expected to ensure efficacy.
No public comments were received regarding the initial regulatory flexibility analysis and no significant issues were raised related to the analysis. Changes from the proposed rule are not expected to change the analyses and findings in the initial regulatory flexibility analysis. No comments were filed by the Chief Counsel for Advocacy of the Small Business Administration in response to the proposed rule.
Given that this action would apply to the entirety of all entities fishing groundfish with bottom longline and pot gear and that the majority are considered small entities, this rule is expected to have an impact on a substantial number of small entities. All open access groundfish fishing vessels are assumed to be small entities, with ex-vessel revenues for all landings (groundfish and non-groundfish) averaging $85,601 in 2023. From 2019-2023, between 72 and 152 vessels harvested groundfish in federal waters in the directed open access fishery using one or both of the subject gears. In 2023, 197 of the 223 federal permit owners or holders (required to fish in the primary or limited entry fixed gear sectors) reported as small entities. For gear switching vessels, using non-trawl gear to harvest groundfish in the Shorebased IFQ Program, of the 10 that participated in 2023, all reported as small entities.
Note that there is not a strict one-to-one correlation between vessels, permits, operators, or entities. Some persons or firms likely have ownership interests in more than one vessel or permit. Multiple permits may be registered for use with a single vessel. Given these factors, the actual number of entities regulated by this action could be lower than the preceding estimates.
All vessels subject to this action would be subject to the new requirements to have lines marked in gear-specific colors (temporary markings allowed for interim period followed by requirements for manufactured lines) and buoys marked with gear specific tags or markings and vessel identification. These requirements are subject to the Paperwork Reduction Act (PRA). It is expected that commercial fishing vessel operators, or their employee(s) or other agent(s), would meet the requirement for line marking by marking the lines with temporary methods (
e.g.,
paint or tape) in the transition period or ordering manufactured lines in the gear-specific color scheme. Vessels are only expected to acquire manufactured line in the required color scheme once during the three-year interim period, as fishing lines often last 6 years or more. The three-year interim period is intended to allow current vertical lines used in the fishery to be phased out and replaced towards the end of their lifespan to avoid unnecessary waste and costs. Additionally, after initial acquisition, replacement of manufactured line in the required color scheme is not expected to increase incremental costs, as compared to what routine gear replacement costs would have been without this new gear marking requirement.
For buoy marking, buoys may be permanently marked directly on the buoy, or cattle ear tags could be ordered and the required identification information etched or stamped on each tag, then affixed to each buoy prior to setting the gear. NMFS estimates that during the 3-year period of this collection, each respondent will only need to purchase tags and line once and then perform ongoing maintenance of those markings.
To annualize gear marking costs, the number of respondents is divided by the 3-year period of this collection, resulting in an average of 112 respondents per year. NMFS estimates it takes approximately 5 hours to replace lines and mark buoys; therefore, the total burden would be approximately 560 hours per year. The estimated average cost burden for compliance with the new gear marking regulations in this rule is estimated to be $809 per respondent (
e.g.,
vessel operator). This total accounts for the costs of gear-specific marked line, gear-specific marked buoy tags, and paint or markers. This cost per vessel does not always equate to the cost per entity.
NMFS does not anticipate any additional compliance burden to the vessels subject to this action from complying with the biodegradable escape panel placement specifications or twine size changes in this rule. This is because industry representatives attest that no retrofitting of existing pots will be required to comply with revised regulations.
Economic impacts from this rulemaking come primarily from the gear marking requirements. The gear marking alternative adopted in the final rule requires marking of only approximately 1 percent of vertical lines; specifically, the portion of the line that is most commonly documented in entanglements. The rulemaking also requires marking every buoy because at least one buoy is observed in the majority of entanglements. For these reasons, the alternative adopted in this final rule provides the best result in terms of assessing minimal costs to industry and providing benefits in terms of being able to positively or negatively attribute entanglements.
There are no expected economic impacts from any other measures in this final rule, including the voluntary single-line allowance to reduce risk of entanglement. The single-line allowance is voluntary in nature to minimize the risk of gear loss, while removing a regulatory barrier to reducing the number of vertical lines in the water. This entanglement risk reduction measure therefore implements NMFS' statutory obligation under the Magnuson-Stevens Act to minimize bycatch to the extent practicable. None of the other alternatives considered during this rulemaking would meet the stated objectives and minimize any significant economic impact of the rule as compared to the final action.
Section 212 of the Small Business Regulatory Enforcement Fairness Act of 1996 (SBREFA) states that, for each rule for which an agency is required to prepare a FRFA, the agency shall publish one or more guides to assist small entities in complying with the rule, and shall designate such publications as “small entity compliance guides.” The agency shall explain the actions a small entity is required to take to comply. As part of this rulemaking process, a notification to permit holders and other interested parties that also serves as small entity compliance guide (the guide) was prepared. Copies of this final rule are available from the West Coast Regional Office, and the guide will be sent electronically to all holders of permits fishing for groundfish in the EEZ with the subject gear types. The guide and this final rule will also be posted to the NMFS website and made available upon request.
Paperwork Reduction Act
This rulemaking contains a collection-of-information requirement subject to review and approval by the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) under the PRA. This rulemaking revises and extends an existing collection with new requirements for fishermen, when using specific gear types to harvest groundfish, to disclose publicly what gear type they are deploying by marking their gear with gear-specific buoy marking and at least the top 20 fm (37 m) of the vertical line in a required color scheme. Line may be either temporarily marked in continuous alternating-colored bands (will only apply for 3 years following the effective date of final rule) or using manufactured line
(
printed page 64804)
with only the two specific colors. Burden estimates for the existing collection, which requires vessel identification on a buoy, are revised to update the estimated number of affected entities with updated fishery information and to adjust cost burden estimates for inflation. Public reporting burden for the vessel identification requirements remains 15 minutes per year per vessel. Public reporting burden for new gear marking requirements that are the subject of this rulemaking is estimated to average 5 hours per year per individual response to gear marking requirements. Burden hour estimates include the time for reviewing instructions, searching equipment sources, gathering and maintaining the equipment needed, and completing and maintaining the collection of information. This collection of information was previously approved by the OMB under OMB Control Number 0648-0352.
One public comment was received directly pertaining to the proposed collection, asking for a correction to an apparent typo in the Supporting Statement and asking NMFS to acknowledge the uncertainty in the burden hour estimates since they were not modeled. No public comments were received regarding: (1) whether this proposed collection of information is necessary for the proper performance of the functions of the agency, including whether the information shall have practical utility; (2) ways to enhance the quality, utility, and clarity of the information to be collected; and (3) ways to minimize the burden of the collection of information, including through the use of automated collection techniques or other forms of information technology.
Notwithstanding any other provision of the law, no person is required to respond to, nor shall any person be subject to a penalty for failure to comply with, a collection of information subject to the requirements of the PRA, unless that collection of information displays a currently valid OMB Control Number.

AGENCY:
National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS), National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), Commerce.
ACTION:
Temporary rule; reallocation.
SUMMARY:
NMFS is reallocating the projected unused amounts of Pacific cod from catcher vessels using trawl gear and catcher/processors using trawl gear to catcher vessels using hook-and-line gear and vessels using pot gear in the Western Regulatory Area of the Gulf of Alaska (GOA). This action is necessary to allow the 2026 total allowable catch (TAC) of Pacific cod to be harvested in the Western Regulatory Area of the GOA.
DATES:
Effective 1200 hours, Alaska local time (A.l.t.), October 13, 2026, through 2400 hours, Alaska local time (A.l.t.), December 31, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Adam Zaleski, 907-586-7228.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
NMFS manages the groundfish fishery in the GOA according to the Fishery Management Plan for Groundfish of the GOA (FMP) prepared and recommended by the North Pacific Fishery Management Council under authority of the Magnuson-Stevens Fishery Conservation and Management Act (Magnuson-Stevens Act). Regulations governing fishing by U.S. vessels in accordance with the FMP appear at subpart H of
50 CFR part 600
and
50 CFR part 679
.
The 2026 Pacific cod TAC allocated to catcher vessels using trawl gear in the Western Regulatory Area of the GOA is 2,506 metric tons (mt), as established by the final 2026 and 2027 harvest specifications for groundfish in the GOA (
91 FR 11902
, March 11, 2026).
The 2026 Pacific cod TAC allocated to catcher/processors using trawl gear in the Western Regulatory Area of the GOA is 157 mt, as established by the final 2026 and 2027 harvest specifications for groundfish in the GOA (
91 FR 11902
, March 11, 2026).
The 2026 Pacific cod TAC allocated to catcher vessels using hook-and-line gear in the Western Regulatory Area of the GOA is 91 mt, as established by the final 2026 and 2027 harvest specifications for groundfish in the GOA (
91 FR 11902
, March 11, 2026).
The 2026 Pacific cod TAC allocated to vessels using pot gear in the Western Regulatory Area of the GOA is 2,480 mt, as established by the final 2026 and 2027 harvest specifications for groundfish in the GOA (
91 FR 11902
, March 11, 2026).
The Administrator, Alaska Region, NMFS (the Administrator) has determined that catcher vessels using trawl gear will not be able to harvest 550 mt of the 2026 Pacific cod TAC allocated to those vessels under § 679.20(a)(12)(i)(A)(
3
) and that catcher/processors using trawl gear will not be able to harvest 100 mt of the 2026 Pacific cod TAC allocated to those vessels under § 679.20(a)(12)(i)(A)(
4
). The Administrator has also determined that catcher vessels using hook-and-line gear have the capability to harvest an additional 250 mt of Pacific cod TAC and vessels using pot gear have the capability to harvest an additional 400 mt of Pacific cod TAC.
Therefore, in accordance with § 679.20(a)(12)(ii)(B), NMFS apportions 550 mt of Pacific cod from catcher vessels using trawl gear and 100 mt of Pacific cod from catcher/processors using trawl gear to the annual amount specified for catcher vessels using hook-and-line gear and to the annual amount specified for vessels using pot gear.
The harvest specifications for 2026 Pacific cod TAC allocated to vessels in the Western Regulatory Area of the GOA included in the final 2026 and 2027 harvest specifications for groundfish in the GOA (
91 FR 11902
, March 11, 2026) is revised as follows: 1,956 mt to catcher vessels using trawl gear, 57 mt to catcher/processors using trawl gear, 341 mt to catcher vessels using hook-and-line gear, and 2,880 mt to vessels using pot gear.
Classification
NMFS issues this action pursuant to section 305(d) of the Magnuson-Stevens Act. This action is required by 50 CFR
(
printed page 64808)
part 679, which was issued pursuant to section 304(b) of the Magnuson-Stevens Act, and is exempt from review under
Executive Order 12866
.
Pursuant to
5 U.S.C. 553(b)(B)
, there is good cause to waive prior notice and an opportunity for public comment on this action, as notice and comment would be impracticable and contrary to the public interest, as it would prevent NMFS from responding to the most recent fisheries data on Pacific cod catch in a timely fashion and would not allow for the full harvest of the Pacific cod TACs by the sectors with harvesting capability. NMFS was unable to publish a notice providing time for public comment because the most recent, relevant data on the harvest of Pacific cod by sectors operating in the Western Regulatory Area of the GOA and the capability of certain sectors to harvest additional TAC only became available as of October 5, 2026.
There is good cause under
5 U.S.C. 553(d)(3)
to waive the 30-day delay in the effective date of this action. This finding is based upon the reasons provided above for waiver of prior notice and opportunity for public comment.

16 U.S.C. 1801
et seq.

AGENCY:
Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), DOT.
ACTION:
Final rule.
SUMMARY:
The FAA is adopting a new airworthiness directive (AD) for all Rolls-Royce Deutschland Ltd & Co KG (RRD) Model RB211 Trent 768-60, 772-60, and 772B-60 engines. This AD was prompted by a report that a batch of low-pressure compressor (LPC) blades were exposed to a non-conforming repair and are more prone to cracking due to a deviation from the approved blade configuration design. This AD requires removal from service of the affected LPC blades and replacement with a serviceable part. The FAA is issuing this AD to address the unsafe condition on these products.
DATES:
This AD is effective November 17, 2026.
The Director of the Federal Register approved the incorporation by reference of a certain publication listed in this AD as of November 17, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
AD Docket:
You may examine the AD docket at
regulations.gov
under Docket No. FAA-2026-4648; or in person at Docket Operations between 9 a.m. and 5 p.m., Monday through Friday, except Federal holidays. The AD docket contains this final rule, the mandatory continuing airworthiness information (MCAI), any comments received, and other information. The address for Docket Operations is U.S. Department of Transportation, Docket Operations, M-30, West Building Ground Floor, Room W12-140, 1200 New Jersey Avenue SE, Washington, DC 20590.
